title: When canonical covariance localisation fails
shortTitle: Where you localise matters: canonical coordinates are not always the best basis
oneLine: Snyder and Hakim's conjecture that canonical coordinates are the best basis for ensemble covariance localisation fails when error is measured in physical variables, at every ensemble size for a single observation, but holds at leading order when error is measured relative to the forecast uncertainty; in their own test case symmetric whitening removes about half the canonical basis's excess error.
abstract: Exact finite-ensemble counterexamples, a sharp leading-order criterion, and the Snyder–Hakim test case. Ensemble Kalman filters estimate forecast uncertainty from a small ensemble and localise the noisy sample covariance, discarding correlations that are probably noise. Snyder and Hakim (2022) conjectured that canonical coordinates (whiten the prior and observation errors, then rotate to the singular vectors of the whitened observation operator) are the best basis in which to localise. For one analysis step with an independent Gaussian ensemble, a known (oracle) prior covariance used to build every basis and deterministic tapers, the answer depends on the loss. Under physical squared error, as in Snyder and Hakim's experiments, a single observation that is not an eigenvector direction of the prior covariance makes the conjecture fail at every ensemble size N ≥ 2: a small rotation followed by complete localisation beats every canonical taper with unit observed diagonal, and with the same deterministic variance rescaling it beats every canonical taper with any observed-variance factor. Two two-dimensional examples are certified in exact rational arithmetic; in one the canonical basis is a strict local maximum of the risk. With several observations, coupling between an observed and an unobserved canonical direction makes canonical complete localisation non-stationary at every N. A uniform large-ensemble expansion gives a leading objective F(U) that ranks bases, and a sharp criterion says exactly when canonical coordinates minimise it; under prior-normalised (Mahalanobis) loss they always do, and for a scalar observation they are a strict local minimum at finite N provided a scalar inequality holds that is supported numerically but unproved. In a reconstruction of Snyder and Hakim's 200-variable test case, canonical coordinates leave about 42–54% of the avoidable excess error, and symmetric (ZCA) whitening does almost as well as the best basis found, equivalent to roughly 1.7–2 times more ensemble members; bases estimated from small pilot samples keep much less of the gain. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Physical squared error, scalar observation (Theorem 3.3, Corollary 3.4, Theorem 3.7, proof): at every ensemble size N ≥ 2, if the observation direction is not an eigenvector of the prior covariance, a small rotation followed by complete localisation beats every canonical taper with unit observed diagonal; with the same deterministic rescaling it also beats every canonical taper with any observed-variance factor.

Exact certificates (Section 4, Appendix A): an explicit rational rotation lowers the risk by at least 1/20416536 at N = 3, and in an aligned example the canonical basis is a strict local maximum of the risk (bounds −56/773 and −508/773).

Several observations (Proposition 5.1, Corollaries 5.2–5.3, proof): compared with rotated complete localisations, canonical complete localisation is not stationary at any N when the loss couples an observed and an unobserved canonical direction, and is stationary when [W, C] = 0; the converse is Conjecture 5.4.

Large ensembles (Theorems 6.1 and 7.1, Corollary 7.6, proof): the leading basis-dependent risk term is 2F(U)/(N−1) with F(U) = Σ(u_iᵀBu_i)(u_iᵀAu_i); canonical coordinates minimise F if and only if A and B commute with oppositely ordered eigenvalues; otherwise they are beaten for all large N. Under prior-normalised loss the criterion always holds.

Snyder–Hakim test case (Section 10, numerical reconstruction): for N = 8 to 64 the best basis found removes 42–54% and symmetric (ZCA) whitening 41–54% of the canonical basis’s excess error over the Kalman filter (N = 8: 1.137 versus 1.063 times the Kalman-filter error), roughly equivalent to 1.7–2 times more ensemble members; canonical is the best found under prior-normalised loss; pilot-estimated bases keep much less of the gain.

narration: Canonical is not always best. An Evidence Press briefing. Weather forecasts are corrected many times a day by combining a model forecast with new observations. To know how much to trust the forecast, forecasters run a small ensemble of forecasts and measure how they differ. With only a few dozen members, the ensemble suggests links between distant places that are just chance. So forecasters use localisation: they throw away the relationships most likely to be noise. How well that works depends on the variables you do it in. In twenty twenty-two, Snyder and Hakim proposed a special set of variables, called canonical coordinates, in which the exact update splits into independent pieces. They conjectured that localising there gives the smallest possible error. This paper finds that the answer depends on how error is measured. Measured in the ordinary physical variables, as in their own experiments, the conjecture fails. With one observation it fails for every ensemble size, unless the observation happens to line up with a principal direction of the forecast uncertainty: a slightly rotated set of variables always does better. With several observations, it fails whenever the scoring links an observed direction with an unobserved one. Measured relative to the forecast's own uncertainty, canonical coordinates are the best choice for large ensembles. The paper also gives a formula that ranks any choice of variables, and a test of exactly when canonical coordinates win. In a reconstruction of Snyder and Hakim's two-hundred-variable test case, with eight members, canonical coordinates give about fourteen per cent more error than an ideal filter. Plain symmetric whitening cuts that to about six per cent, which is like doubling the ensemble. These results assume the true forecast uncertainty is known and look at a single update; when it has to be estimated from a small sample, much of the gain disappears. The proofs, exact certificates and code are openly archived. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, not peer reviewed or independently reproduced. Published on the third of November twenty twenty-six, its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

decisionObject.description: Whether canonical coordinates are the best basis in which to apply complete covariance localisation in an ensemble Kalman analysis: yes at leading order under prior-normalised loss; under physical loss only when A and B commute with oppositely ordered eigenvalues (Theorem 7.1), and never at finite N for a scalar observation that is not a prior eigenvector direction.
decisionObject.scope: One analysis step, independent Gaussian ensemble, oracle prior covariance used to build every basis, deterministic tapers, quadratic loss. Cycling, estimated covariances, adaptive localisation and operational data are not covered.
